stories.excerpt: The instinct to fix things for our kids is all too human. Parents are hardwired to do our best to clear any roadblocks from their path. This impulse served humans well for millennia when such roadblocks were much more likely to be a matter of life or death. But fast-forward to today, an age of relative safety and comfort for many, and this instinct may no longer be serving us. Making matters worse is that we live in an age of so-called experts offering an ever-growing pool of advice on how to resolve any challenges children are facing. Mind you, we may never have considered these challenges as a problem in the first place. Think, for example, about our intense drive to optimize kids’ diets. stories.title: Rent-a-grandchild: Businesses offering companions to elderly grow in India
stories.description: A small but growing number of firms selling what families once took for granted: someone to take care of the seniors.
stories.excerpt: A small but growing number of companies are selling what families once took for granted: someone to take care of the ageing people. New Delhi, India – Both daughters of S Budhiraja live in the United States. Yet, when he and his wife head out to the market in Gurugram, a bustling business district on the outskirts of India’s capital, a young man walks beside them. Across Indian cities, a small but growing number of companies are now selling what families once took for granted: someone to take care of ageing people. Chores include taking them to the temple, sitting with them during a hospital visit, playing cards, or simply listening to them. Some firms call such workers “children for hire”; others call them a “grandchild for rent”. India, the world’s most populous country, is growing older quickly. Lagos, Nigeria – Half an hour after Nurudeen Sanni and his crew began shooting a documentary in Ajah, several men surrounded them and demanded 100,000 naira (about $75) before they could continue filming. As the crew negotiated, one of the men slapped a crew member who tried to protect the cameras. A scuffle broke out, and the men produced knives and cutlasses. The crew fled, but one member was stabbed in the neck and seriously injured, Sanni said. “The painful part was that we saw a member of our crew being beaten and we could not do anything,” said Sanni, a 40-year-old sound recordist. stories.excerpt: Croatian police say that at least two people were killed and several were injured when a bus overturned on a highway ZAGREB, Croatia -- At least two people were killed and several were injured when a bus overturned on a highway in Croatia on Sunday, police said. The bus with Serbian license plates skidded off the road and overturned at 7:25 a.m. while traveling in the direction of the Croatian capital, Zagreb, police said. The reason for the accident was not immediately clear. The A3 highway in Croatia leads from the Serbian border, by Zagreb and toward Slovenia. Emergency services said that 33 passengers and two drivers were on the bus when it crashed. Around 20 people have been injured, some seriously, Dario Kezeric, Zagreb county firefighters' commander, told the state HRT broadcaster. Photos from the scene carried by local media showed a broken road fence and the bus lying on the side by the road. A helicopter was also called to the scene, the HRT report said.

stories.title: EXPLAINED: Italian inheritance law and second homes
stories.description: Italian inheritance laws are substantially different to those in many English-speaking countries. Here's what second-home owners in Italy need to know about succession laws and inheritance tax.
stories.excerpt: Italian inheritance laws are substantially different to those in many English-speaking countries. Here's what second-home owners in Italy need to know about succession laws and inheritance tax. The situation when it comes to both inheritance law and inheritance tax can be complicated for second-home owners, especially those who own property in Italy but live in another country. For starters, the most notable difference between Italian inheritance law and that of many English-speaking countries is the concept of 'forced heirs', or eredi legittimari. Several family members have protected rights under Italian law to inherit a portion of the estate of a late family member. These include a spouse or civil partner, children, and parents or grandparents if you don’t have children. A portion of your estate has to go to these heirs. This is called the reserved share (quota di legittima). There’s also a disposable share (quota disponibile) of your estate which can go to anyone, relative or not.
